parts.text:
35 The circuit shown contains a cell with negligible internal resistance.
X
The energy transferred per unit charge in driving charge around the complete circuit is E. The
potential difference (p.d.) across X is V.
The cell is then replaced with a different cell of the same electromotive force (e.m.f.) that has
significant internal resistance.
What is the effect on E and V of replacing the cell?
effect on E
effect on V
A
decreases
decreases
B
decreases
increases
C
no change
decreases
D
no change
increases

hints: Notice the wording for $E$: energy transferred per unit charge in driving charge around the complete circuit is the definition of e.m.f., not terminal p.d.
Recall that the p.d. across external resistor X is the terminal p.d., given by $V = \text{e.m.f.} - Ir$ when the cell has internal resistance $r$ and current $I$.
Compare the two cells: same e.m.f. means same $E$, but the second cell diverts some of that energy per charge to its own internal resistance, leaving less per charge for X.
walkthrough: Identify $E$ from its definition: work done by the cell per unit charge driven around the whole circuit. That is the e.m.f. of the cell.
The new cell is stated to have the same e.m.f., so $E$ must show no change even though internal resistance is now significant.
Identify $V$ as the terminal p.d. across the external resistor X. With the first cell of negligible internal resistance, $V$ is essentially equal to the e.m.f.
With significant internal resistance $r$, the closed circuit carries current $I$ and there is lost volts $Ir$ inside the cell, so $V = \text{e.m.f.} - Ir$.
Since $Ir > 0$, the energy per charge delivered to X is smaller, so $V$ decreases while $E$ is unchanged. This is option C.

A.explanation: E does not decrease because E is the e.m.f. and the replacement cell has the same e.m.f.

B.explanation: E stays the same for the same e.m.f., and V cannot increase because some potential is now lost inside the cell.

C.explanation: E is the e.m.f. so it is unchanged, while V is the terminal p.d. and it falls because of the lost volts $Ir$ across the internal resistance.

D.explanation: E is unchanged, but V does not increase because the larger total resistance reduces the current and part of the e.m.f. is dropped across the internal resistance.
